old.name: Champagne — grower fizz (the closest real vineyard to Paris)
old.hook: The grande-marque names on the boulevard ads are blends and marketing, not a place. RM means one family grew the grapes and bottled the wine from its own village, roughly ninety minutes east of the Gare de l'Est — about the nearest true terroir Paris pours. Read the fine print by the cork wire; that two-letter code tells you more than the label ever will.

old.name: Chablis & Sancerre — the two bistro whites by the glass
old.hook: The default un verre de blanc splits two ways. Chablis is chardonnay grown on Kimmeridgian marl — a roughly 150-million-year-old seabed still full of fossil oyster shells — and in its classic village form sees no new oak. Sancerre is sauvignon on Loire flint; that struck-match, gunflint smell has a name, pierre à fusil. Both live or die on a saline, chalky edge, so skip anything buttery or oaked.

old.name: Beaujolais — the natural, chilled red
old.hook: Forget the November nouveau; this is serious cru gamay (Morgon, Fleurie, Chiroubles) with little or no added sulphur. It's arguably where the modern natural-wine revival took root in the 1980s, under the influence of the chemist and researcher Jules Chauvet. Ask for it lightly chilled — twenty minutes in the fridge — and the whole-cluster ferment gives that lifted, crushed-cherry rush that makes people drink the bottle too fast.

old.name: Cidre & Poiré — the honest outsider
old.hook: Honesty first: Paris is not cider country. This is the drink of Normandy and Brittany, and it belongs beside a buckwheat galette, not on a Champs-Élysées terrace. Bordelet, a former sommelier at three-star L'Arpège, makes bottle-fermented cidre that drinks closer to fine wine than beer — look for 'brut' and méthode ancestrale. One thing to know: poiré is pear, not apple.

old.name: Pastis — the Marseille drink Paris pours out of habit
old.hook: Say it plainly: pastis is Provence and the Vieux-Port, not Parisian terroir — the zinc-bar terrasse serves it on reflex. Cut roughly five parts iced water to one, and watch it turn milky: the anise oils drop out of solution, the louche. That cloud is the whole ritual. (Aside for the curious: Paris does have a licensed still again — Distillerie de Paris, opened 2015 and billed as the first legal distillery in the capital since 1914 — though its output is gin, whisky and rum, not pastis.)

old.name: Café crème — the breakfast-only milk coffee
old.hook: The big milky coffee is a morning thing and only a morning thing: order one after lunch and every waiter clocks you as a visitor. Past noon, Parisians switch to un express (a short black) or un noisette (espresso cut with a drop of milk). It is not a cappuccino — no latte art, no oat milk unless you're somewhere new-wave. The teachable half-second: 'un crème', not 'a coffee with milk'.

old.name: Bar Hemingway, Ritz Paris
old.hook: A tiny wood-panelled cocktail room at the back of the Ritz, hung with the writer's photographs, where the martini is treated as scripture.
old.text: A tiny wood-panelled cocktail room at the back of the Ritz, hung with the writer's photographs, where the martini is treated as scripture. The room's history dates to 1921 and it passed through several names — Le Petit Bar, Bar Bertin — before taking Hemingway's, after the legend that he 'liberated' the German-occupied Ritz in 1944 by marching in and running up a tab for fifty-one dry martinis. It went dark in 1982 and stayed shut twelve years, reopening in 1994 under head barman Colin Field, whom Forbes once called the best bartender alive; he built its reputation on cocktails mixed to your mood, not a menu. The one real thing to know: it is tiny — around twenty-five seats, no reservations, arrive at opening (6pm) or queue. Signal Room dates to 1921; reopened 1994 under Colin Field (still head barman in 2026)

old.name: Le Bar du Bristol
old.hook: A jewel-box corner bar in Le Bristol designed as a cabinet of curiosities, where cocktails come with petits fours and, on weekend nights, a DJ.
old.text: A jewel-box corner bar in Le Bristol designed as a cabinet of curiosities, where cocktails come with petits fours and, on weekend nights, a DJ. Le Bristol opened in April 1925 on the Faubourg Saint-Honoré, the street of the Élysée Palace and the couture houses, and has always drawn a diplomatic-and-fashion crowd. The bar as it stands is comparatively young — inaugurated in 2012 — and was styled to feel like a collector's study rather than a hotel lounge, all curiosities and low light, with contemporary-art video playing behind the bar. The thing worth knowing: it is quietly one of the few grand-hotel bars in Paris with a genuine late crowd and music (its weekend 'Bristol After Dark' sets), not just hushed reverence. Signal Hotel opened April 1925; bar inaugurated 2012

old.name: Bar Joséphine, Hôtel Lutetia
old.hook: The frescoed grand bar of the Left Bank's only 'Palace'-distinction hotel, named for Josephine Baker, with regular live jazz.
old.text: The frescoed grand bar of the Left Bank's only 'Palace'-distinction hotel, named for Josephine Baker, with regular live jazz. The Lutetia opened in 1910, built by the owners of Le Bon Marché to lodge their department-store clients — the first luxury hotel on the Left Bank, later a haunt of Picasso, Joyce and Saint-Exupéry, and in 2019 the only Left Bank hotel to win France's official 'Palace' label. During the 2014–2018 restoration, workers uncovered the bar's original 1910 ceiling-and-wall frescoes by Adrien Karbowsky, hidden for decades under coats of paint and a veil of white-painted glass; they were painstakingly brought back over roughly 17,000 hours. The one real thing: it earns its name honestly with a strong jazz programme, so time a visit to a live set. Signal 1910 hotel; Karbowsky frescoes found under paint and painted glass, restored by 2018; Left Bank's only Palace (2019)
